title: Chicago's food inspection forecasting model finds critical violations 7.5 days earlier in a double-blind retrodiction
summary: Double-blind retrodiction of 1,637 Chicago inspections (Sept-Oct 2014): the model would have found 69% of critical-violation sites in the first half of the work versus 55%, 7.5 days earlier.
account: Chicago's Department of Innovation and Technology and Department of Public Health built a model. Pro bono data scientists from Allstate Insurance and the Civic Consulting Alliance helped. It assigns each of the city's 15,000+ food establishments a likelihood of a critical violation. Predictors include previous critical or serious violations, three-day average high temperature, nearby garbage and sanitation complaints and facility type. Others are nearby burglaries, licenses, time since last inspection, length of operation and the inspector assigned. In a double-blind retrodiction, the Department of Public Health inspected 1,637 establishments in its normal order during September and October 2014. Of these, 258 (almost 16%) had at least one critical violation, 141 (55%) found in the first month. Re-ordering the same inspections by the model's probabilities would have found 178 (69%) in the first half of the work, on average 7.5 days earlier. Another 37 would have been cited in the first month. The Harvard Ash Center's Data-Smart City Solutions wrote up the pilot on 19 May 2015. The city page is undated. The code is open source in R.
purpose: Forecast which Chicago food establishments are most likely to have critical sanitation violations so that inspectors visit them first.
system: Food Inspection Forecasting (predictive analytics model, open-sourced in R)
developer: City of Chicago Department of Innovation and Technology with the Department of Public Health, Allstate Insurance data scientists and the Civic Consulting Alliance

ratings.reason: The sources document a retrospective simulation (69% vs 55% found in the first half; 7.5 days earlier) and no live-deployment outcome.
Earlier discovery “potentially after patrons became ill” is stated as a rationale. No illness outcome is documented.

ai_role.statement: Developer and deployer are the same body. The City of Chicago built the model in-house with pro bono partners and the Department of Public Health is the user. The evaluation re-scored inspections after they were completed, so the model did not change any inspection in the pilot. Model type is not stated in the sources.

headline: Chicago's model finds critical violations 7.5 days earlier
metric: 69% of critical-violation sites in the first half of the work versus 55%, 7.5 days earlier

comparator.against: the Department of Public Health's normal inspection order during the September-October 2014 pilot
comparator.before: 55 percent (141 establishments) of those with critical violations found in the first month during normal operations
comparator.after: 69 percent (178 establishments) found in the first half of work; violations found on average 7 and a half days earlier
comparator.quote: During the simulation, 69 percent of inspections—178 establishments—with critical violations were found during the first half of work, compared to 55 percent during normal operations. Over the two month pilot, establishments with violations were found, on average, 7 and a half days earlier.

later.note: An independent 2019 hindsight analysis states that CDPH deployed the model in 2015 to schedule inspections of Chicago's 15,000-plus food establishments and released the training data and code.
later.quote: In 2015, CDPH deployed a machine learning model to schedule inspections of establishments based on their likelihood to commit critical food code violations. The City of Chicago released the training data and source code for the model, allowing anyone to examine the model.
